questions.stem: What are the two main transport tissues in plants?
questions.explanation: The two main transport tissues in plants are xylem (transports water and minerals upward) and phloem (transports sugars in both directions).

options.text: Water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to leaves

questions.explanation: Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots upward through the stem to the leaves, driven mainly by transpiration.

options.text: Dissolved sugars (sucrose) from sources to sinks

questions.explanation: Phloem transports dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) and amino acids from where they are produced (sources, e.g., leaves) to where they are needed or stored (sinks, e.g., roots, fruits).

questions.stem: What is the process of water transport in xylem called?
questions.explanation: The movement of water from roots through xylem to leaves is called the transpiration stream. It is driven by the evaporation of water from leaves (transpiration).

options.text: The transport of dissolved sugars in phloem from source to sink
The movement of water in xylem
The absorption of minerals by roots
The evaporation of water from leaves

questions.explanation: Translocation is the transport of dissolved organic substances (mainly sucrose) through phloem tissue from sources (where sugars are made) to sinks (where they are used or stored).

questions.stem: In which direction does water move through the xylem?

options.text: Upward only, from roots to leaves

questions.explanation: Water moves upward through xylem from the roots to the leaves. This movement is driven by transpiration pull from above and root pressure from below.

questions.stem: Why do plants need a transport system?

options.text: Because they are too large for diffusion alone to supply all cells with water and nutrients

questions.explanation: Plants need a transport system because their large size means diffusion alone would be too slow to supply all cells with the water, minerals, and sugars they need for survival.
